title: When Does Task-Aware Imputation Matter? An Analysis of Robustness Under Train–Test Mismatch

paper.title: When Does Task-Aware Imputation Matter? An Analysis of Robustness Under Train–Test Mismatch
paper.abstract:
Abstract Missing data is a pervasive challenge in machine learning, often degrading predictive performance and complicating model deployment. Most existing approaches treat imputation as a preprocessing step independent of the downstream task, a separation that becomes problematic under train–test mismatches in missingness mechanisms or rates. We introduce a unified framework that treats missing entries as variables in a task-conditioned optimization problem. We instantiate this framework in two settings: an amortized approach for scenarios with missing data at both training and test time, and a latent optimization approach for settings where only training data is incomplete.
The evaluation is conducted on 98 tabular datasets and robustness under train–test mismatches is assessed on 36 datasets.
Results reveal that reconstruction error constitutes a poor proxy for predictive utility (Spearman ρ ≈ \rho\approx 0.16–0.32), and that task-aware imputation becomes critical in scenarios where classical methods fail to recover complete-data performance, achieving win rates of up to 80% in challenging train–test mismatch scenarios.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Missing data is a pervasive problem in real-world machine learning, with significant implications for the validity, reliability, and fairness of predictive models. In practice, data may be incomplete due to collection errors, equipment failures, participant drop-out, or reluctance to disclose sensitive information. Missing values can lead to biased estimates, reduced statistical power, and degraded performance, making their handling a critical component of any data-driven pipeline. Understanding why data is missing– the missingness mechanism– is essential. There are three main missingness mechanisms: Missing Completely At Random (MCAR), where the probability of missingness is independent of the data; Missing At Random (MAR), where the probability of missingness is independent of the missing values given the observed data; and Missing Not At Random (MNAR), where the probability of missingness depends on the unobserved values themselves [ 1 , 2 ] . These mechanisms not only influence how missing data should be modeled, but also interact with when missingness occurs in the learning pipeline. In practice, an important consideration is whether missingness occurs at inference time. In some applications, missing values appear only during training, while deployment data is clean [ 2 ] . In others, missingness persists at test time, often under shifts in mechanisms or rates [ 3 , 4 ] . These scenarios pose distinct challenges: the former primarily affects representation learning, while the latter requires robustness to distribution shift. Despite these differences, most imputation methods treat missing data as a static preprocessing problem, without explicitly accounting for when or how missingness occurs. This raises a fundamental question: to what extent does improving imputation quality translate into better predictive performance, particularly in realistic settings where missingness persists at test time or differs between training and deployment? This question leads to the primary goal of this work, which is to investigate when task-aware imputation improves predictive performance in supervised learning with missing values. Our contributions are threefold. First, we show that task-aware imputation is not universally beneficial, but instead becomes critical in challenging regimes such as distribution shift and intrinsically hard missingness settings. Second, we introduce a simple and flexible formulation that treats missing values as learnable variables jointly optimized with the predictive model, providing a common perspective that encompasses both amortized and latent approaches within a single framework. Third, through a comprehensive empirical study, we demonstrate that standard reconstruction metrics are only weakly correlated with downstream performance, highlighting the limitations of conventional evaluation protocols.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Approaches to handling missing data include imputation, where missing entries are filled; omission, where incomplete samples are discarded; and methods that directly operate on incomplete data [ 2 , 5 , 6 ] . In this work, we focus on imputation. Classical methods such as mean, median, and K K -NN [ 7 ] are simple and efficient but fail to capture complex dependencies. Iterative approaches such as MissForest [ 8 ] , MICE [ 9 ] , and related conditional models [ 10 ] model non-linear relationships but are computationally expensive and sensitive to design choices. HyperImpute [ 11 ] extends this paradigm through automated model and hyperparameter selection, while low-rank matrix completion methods exploit global structure [ 12 , 13 ] . Learning-based approaches such as TabPFN [ 14 ] and TabImpute [ 15 ] leverage pretrained models for fast, zero-shot imputation. Deep learning methods for tabular data, including transformer-based architectures [ 16 , 17 ] , have further advanced this direction. Several approaches model the joint data distribution using deep generative models [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 ] , learning to reconstruct missing entries through reconstruction objectives, often with masking strategies during training. While expressive, these methods typically prioritize data fidelity over downstream predictive performance. Other works incorporate additional structure into the imputation process. For instance, MIRACLE [ 27 ] models the missingness mechanism under MNAR using causal assumptions, while optimal transport-based approaches align distributions between observed and missing data [ 28 , 29 ] . Handling missing data in supervised learning has traditionally relied on two-stage pipelines, where missing values are first imputed and then used for downstream prediction. This separation can lead to suboptimal performance, as imputation is not aligned with the predictive task. Benchmark studies show that the choice of imputation method significantly affects downstream performance, particularly in terms of robustness and interpretability [ 30 ] . Moreover, standard metrics such as RMSE and MAE often fail to reflect imputation quality, as they do not capture discrepancies in the underlying data distribution. Task-aware approaches aim to address this limitation. TARImpute [ 31 ] co-optimizes imputation with clustering objectives, while OptImpute [ 32 ] formulates imputation as an optimization problem independent of downstream supervision. Deep learning methods such as GRAPE [ 33 ] and GEDI [ 34 ] propose end-to-end frameworks that jointly perform imputation and prediction, often relying on specific architectural choices such as graph-based representations. Changes in missingness mechanisms can also induce distribution shift. Domain Adaptation under Missingness Shift (DAMS) [ 3 ] shows that differences in missingness alone can invalidate standard assumptions and require adaptation, particularly when missingness indicators are unavailable. Similarly, StableMiss+ [ 4 ] studies mask distribution shifts and proposes removing unstable correlations involving the missingness mask. These works highlight two key challenges: (i) robustness under shifts in missingness mechanisms or rates, and (ii) the misalignment between imputation quality and downstream predictive performance. We address these challenges by introducing a unified formulation that treats missing values as learnable variables jointly trained with the predictive model. This perspective directly aligns imputation with the task objective, and allows us to characterize when such alignment translates into improved predictive performance. Unlike prior task-aware approaches, our formulation does not depend on specific architectures or specialized designs (e.g., graph-based models), and avoids the need for bilevel optimization. Instead, it provides a simple and flexible lens to study task-aware imputation itself, encompassing both per-sample (latent) and amortized strategies within a single formulation. Furthermore, we explicitly investigate train–test mismatches in missingness mechanisms and rates, a setting that remains largely underexplored in existing work.

sections.heading: 4 Experimental Setup
sections.text: We evaluate the proposed framework under two complementary settings reflecting different practical scenarios regarding the availability of missing values at inference time. In our experiments, we focus on classification tasks , therefore we use the Cross-Entropy (CE) loss. For more details on the classifier, refer to Appendix A.5 .

sections.heading: Joint-AmortizedImpute: missingness at inference time.
sections.text: This constitutes our main evaluation setting. We consider three scenarios to assess robustness under distribution shifts in missingness: • Robustness under train/test mismatch. – Same mechanism, different missing rates: The missingness mechanism is fixed (either MCAR, MAR or MNAR), whereas the missing rate differs between training m r train ∈ { 0.1 , 0.3 } m_{r}^{\text{train}}\in\{0.1,0.3\} and testing m r test ∈ { 0.1 , 0.3 , 0.5 , 0.7 } : m r test ≠ m r train m_{r}^{\text{test}}\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7\}:m_{r}^{\text{test}}\neq m_{r}^{\text{train}} . – Different mechanism, same missing rate: The missing rate is fixed ( m r train = m r test ∈ { 0.1 , 0.5 } m_{r}^{\text{train}}=m_{r}^{\text{test}}\in\{0.1,0.5\} ), while the missingness mechanism varies between training and testing (MCAR, MAR or MNAR). • Overall stability. Training and test data share the same missingness mechanism and rate. We evaluate six missignness mechanisms– MCAR; MAR and its sequential variant; MNAR, and its latent-factor and polarization variants– across five missing rates, m r ∈ { 0.1 , 0.3 , 0.5 , 0.7 , 0.8 } m_{r}\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.8\} .

sections.heading: Joint-LatentImpute: no missingness at inference time.
sections.text: This setting isolates the effect of task-aware imputation during training while reflecting scenarios where training data is incomplete but deployment data is clean. We evaluate across the same six missingness mechanisms (MCAR; MAR and its sequential variant; and MNAR with latent-factor and polarization variants) and five missing rates m r ∈ { 0.1 , 0.3 , 0.5 , 0.7 , 0.8 } m_{r}\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.8\} . Please, refer to Appendix A.3 for more details on data splits and simulated missingness mechanisms.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare the proposed approach with the following imputation methods : mean/median for continuous variables, mode for categorical variables, K K -NN using the mean of the nearest neighbors for numerical variables and mode imputation for categorical ones, MissForest and TabImpute. We also consider the complete data baseline, which provides an upper bound on performance and allows us to quantify the impact of missingness and imputation.

sections.heading: Reference imputation choice.
sections.text: We select the reference imputation 𝐱 ^ u \hat{\mathbf{x}}^{\text{u}} using a task-driven procedure: each candidate method is used to impute the training data, a downstream classifier is trained, and the method yielding the best validation performance is chosen. This selection is performed per dataset and missingness setting and provides a strong initialization for the proposed method, improving stability and focusing learning on task-relevant corrections.

sections.heading: Evaluation metrics.
sections.text: Imputation quality is measured using Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) for numerical features and error rate for categorical features (Cat. Err.). To assess downstream utility, we train a classifier on the imputed data and report accuracy/F1-score. We report the performance gap relative to the complete-data baseline: Gap = Accuracy complete-data − Accuracy method . \mathrm{Gap}=\mathrm{Accuracy}_{\text{complete-data}}-\mathrm{Accuracy}_{\text{method}}. (11) Lower values indicate better performance, with a gap of zero corresponding to perfect recovery. We additionally measure performance recovery using the recovery ratio , defined as the ratio between the accuracy obtained under missing data and the accuracy achieved on the corresponding complete-data baseline: RR = Accuracy method Accuracy complete-data . \mathrm{RR}=\frac{\mathrm{Accuracy}_{\text{method}}}{\mathrm{Accuracy}_{\text{complete-data}}}. (12) A value of RR = 1 \mathrm{RR}=1 indicates full recovery of complete-data performance, while lower values reflect degradation due to missingness. Values greater than 1 indicate that the method outperforms the complete-data baseline. sections.heading: Best classical method.
sections.text: For reporting purposes, we define the best classical method in each scenario as the imputation approach achieving the highest test accuracy. This definition is used only for post-hoc comparison and does not affect model selection, which is performed using validation performance.

sections.heading: Datasets and data preprocessing.
sections.text: We evaluate our approach on classification datasets from OpenML [ 35 ] . For experiments involving distribution shifts (cross-mechanism and varying missing-rate), we use a set of 36 datasets with imbalance ratio below 10 to avoid severely skewed class distributions. In this setting, classification performance is evaluated using accuracy. To assess overall robustness and stability, including hardness analysis unrelated to distribution shifts, we extend the evaluation to a broader collection of 98 datasets. All methods are evaluated on identical data splits to ensure fair comparison. Numerical features are standardized using z-score normalization, where statistics are computed using only observed values from the training set. Further details on dataset characteristics and domains are provided in Appendix 11 .

sections.heading: Statistical analysis.
sections.text: To assess statistical significance across multiple datasets, we follow standard protocols for comparing learning algorithms. Methods are ranked per dataset and compared using the Friedman test, followed by the Nemenyi post-hoc test to identify significant differences in average rank. We visualize results using critical difference (CD) diagrams, where lower ranks indicate better performance and horizontal bars connect methods that are not significantly different. Additionally, we report Spearman rank correlations to analyze the relationship between reconstruction quality and downstream performance. All statistical tests are conducted at a significance level of α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 .

sections.heading: Joint-LatentImpute.
sections.text: We analyze the relationship between imputation quality and downstream classification performance using Spearman rank correlation between RMSE ranks and accuracy ranks across all scenarios. We observe a statistically significant positive correlation (Spearman, ρ = 0.16 \rho=0.16 , p < 0.001 p<0.001 ), which indicates that methods achieving better reconstruction quality tend to also perform better in downstream prediction. However, this correlation is weak, suggesting that reconstruction error alone does not fully explain predictive performance. For example, MissForest achieves competitive performance in terms of numerical reconstruction error, ranking second overall. However, this advantage does not translate to downstream classification performance, where simpler methods such as mean and K-NN imputation often perform better.

sections.heading: Conclusions.
sections.text: This work studies the role of task-aware imputation in supervised learning with missing data, with a focus on understanding when it improves predictive performance. Our results show that task-aware imputation does not uniformly improve predictive performance, but instead provides benefits primarily in challenging regimes , particularly under distribution shift and in MNAR settings, where classical methods fail to recover complete-data performance. We further find that reconstruction quality is only weakly correlated with downstream performance (Spearman ρ ≈ \rho\approx 0.16–0.32), suggesting that optimizing imputation for reconstruction alone is insufficient. These results indicate that imputation should be treated as a task-dependent problem , rather than a preprocessing step focused solely on data fidelity.

sections.heading: Limitations and Future Work.
sections.text: The proposed Joint-AmortizedImpute approach uses fixed hyperparameters across all datasets. While this ensures consistent evaluation, it may limit adaptability; dataset-specific tuning or automated optimization could improve performance and robustness. The experimental comparison is also limited to a small set of baseline methods, and extending the benchmark would enable a more comprehensive evaluation. Furthermore, experiments focus exclusively on tabular classification, leaving generalization to other settings (e.g., regression or structured data such as time series) as an open question. Finally, the method does not explicitly model the missingness mechanism, which may reduce effectiveness when missingness is structured or informative. Incorporating mechanism-aware components is a promising direction for future work.

sections.heading: Broader impacts.
sections.text: Improved handling of missing data can enhance the reliability of machine learning systems in real-world applications such as healthcare, finance, and scientific analysis. By aligning imputation with predictive objectives, the proposed approach may support better decision-making. However, task-aware imputation may also amplify biases in the observed data, leading to unfair or misleading outcomes, particularly in sensitive domains. Future work should explore fairness-aware imputation and develop safeguards to mitigate these risks.

sections.heading: A.3 Data splits and missingness
sections.text: Each dataset is split into training (70%), validation (15%), and test (15%) sets using stratified sampling with respect to the class labels. Splits are generated using a fixed random seed (42) to ensure reproducibility. Categorical variables are encoded as integer category codes prior to missingness generation. Missing values are introduced after splitting the data, independently for the training, validation and test sets. Other than the classical MCAR, MAR, and MNAR settings, we consider three additional missingness mechanisms capturing different dependency structures. These mechanisms are implemented using the TabImpute framework [ 15 ] , which provides configurable generators for structured missingness patterns. MAR Sequential is generated using an ϵ \epsilon -greedy bandit process, where missingness depends on previously observed values. MNAR latent factor missingness is driven by a low-rank latent representation of the data, making missingness depend on unobserved variables. In particular, the latent rank is randomly sampled between 1 and 5, introducing variability in the underlying dependency structure. MNAR Polarization missingness preferentially removes values in the lower tail of the distribution (below the 25th percentile), simulating censoring effects.

sections.heading: A.4 Benchmark imputation methods
sections.text: For each dataset and missingness configuration, we load both the fully observed data and the corresponding corrupted version with missing values. A binary mask indicating observed entries is also provided. Numerical features are standardized using a StandardScaler fitted on the training data and applied to all splits. We evaluate five imputation methods: mean, median, K K -NN, MissForest and TabImpute. Numerical and categorical features are handled separately when required, with categorical variables typically imputed using the mode. If a categorical feature contains only missing values, a default value (0) is assigned. Numerical features are standardized using a StandardScaler fitted on the training data with missing values. The same transformation is applied to validation and test sets. Categorical variables are represented as integer-encoded categories during imputation. After imputation, all features are transformed using one-hot encoding before being passed to the classifier. Each imputation method is applied independently to the training, validation, and test sets. For methods requiring fitting, the imputer is trained on the training data and then applied to validation and test sets. Specifically: • Mean and median imputation are computed exclusively on the training data. For numerical features, the mean or median of each feature is calculated using the training set and used to fill missing values. For categorical features, the mode is used. The same statistics are then consistently applied to validation and test sets through feature encoding alignment. • K K -NN imputation (implemented with sklearn.impute.KNNImputer ) is fitted on the numerical features of the training data only. Missing numerical values are imputed based on nearest neighbors in the training set with K = 5 K=5 . Categorical features are imputed separately using the training-set mode. • MissForest (implemented via the missforest package https://github.com/yuenshingyan/MissForest ) is trained exclusively on the training data. A random forest model is iteratively fitted to predict missing values using observed features, and the trained imputer is then used to reconstruct the training data. • TabImpute (using tabimpute.interface.TabImputeCategorical [ 15 ] ) is applied independently to each data split. The same hyperparameters are used across splits, but the model does not reuse information from the training set when imputing validation or test data. TabImpute processes data in chunks, with a maximum of 64 rows per chunk and up to 4 chunks per batch. After imputation, categorical variables are one-hot encoded, and a classifier is trained on the imputed training data. For each dataset and missingness configuration, the imputation method yielding the highest validation accuracy is selected. Imputation quality is assessed by comparing imputed values to ground truth using a masked error metric computed only on missing entries. Imputation time is recorded to assess computational efficiency. For reproducibility, results and best-performing imputations are stored for each dataset, mechanism, and missingness level.

sections.heading: A.5 Classifier
sections.text: For all experiments, we use a simple feedforward neural network to isolate the effect of the proposed imputation method. The classifier consists of a single hidden layer with ReLU activation: f θ ​ ( x ) = W 2 ​ σ ​ ( W 1 ​ x + b 1 ) + b 2 , f_{\theta}(x)=W_{2}\,\sigma(W_{1}x+b_{1})+b_{2}, (14) where σ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \sigma(\cdot) denotes the ReLU activation. The hidden dimension is fixed to h = 32 h=32 across all experiments. The classifier is intentionally kept lightweight to ensure that performance differences are primarily attributable to the imputation strategy rather than model capacity.

sections.heading: Implementation details.
sections.text: Model parameters are initialized using Kaiming uniform initialization for linear layers. Missing numerical entries are initialized from the reference values with additive Gaussian noise 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 0.1 2 ) \mathcal{N}(0,0.1^{2}) . For categorical features, missing values are initialized by sampling from a noisy version of the reference distribution, obtained via a softmax over perturbed log-probabilities. Observed categorical values are encoded as smoothed one-hot vectors. Optimization is performed using Adam with separate learning rates for model parameters and latent variables: respectively, 1 × 10 − 3 1\times 10^{-3} and 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} . Gradients are clipped to a maximum norm of 5 to ensure stability. Early stopping is applied with a patience of 50 iterations. Mini-batch training is used with batch size 64. The Gumbel-Softmax temperature is annealed exponentially during training from 1.0 to a minimum of 0.2. All experiments are conducted using a fixed random seed (42) for reproducibility.

sections.text: Let P classifier P_{\text{classifier}} be the number of parameters of the downstream classification model, d num d_{\text{num}} the number of missing numerical entries, and d cat d_{\text{cat}} the number of latent parameters associated with categorical missing entries. sections.heading: Computational Complexity.
sections.text: Let n n be the number of samples, d d the input dimensionality, h h the hidden dimension of the classifier, and T T the number of training iterations. In this approach, missing values are treated as free optimization variables, resulting in 𝒪 ⁡ ( | ℳ | ) \mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{M}|) additional parameters, where ℳ \mathcal{M} denotes the set of missing entries. Each training iteration requires a forward and backward pass through the classifier, with complexity 𝒪 ⁡ ( d ​ h + h 2 ) \mathcal{O}(dh+h^{2}) per sample, as well as updates to the latent variables, which incur an additional cost proportional to | ℳ | |\mathcal{M}| . The overall training complexity is therefore: 𝒪 ⁡ ( T ⋅ ( n b ⋅ ( d ​ h + h 2 ) + | ℳ | ) ) , \mathcal{O}\left(T\cdot\left(\frac{n}{b}\cdot(dh+h^{2})+|\mathcal{M}|\right)\right), (26) which becomes 𝒪 ⁡ ( T ⋅ n ​ d ) \mathcal{O}(T\cdot nd) in the worst case. The space complexity is 𝒪 ⁡ ( n ​ d + | ℳ | ) \mathcal{O}(nd+|\mathcal{M}|) , dominated by storing the dataset and the latent variables.

sections.heading: A.7 Joint-AmortizedImpute
sections.text: Given an input with missing values X X , a mask M ∈ { 0 , 1 } d M\in\{0,1\}^{d} indicating observed entries, and a reference imputation Z ref Z_{\text{ref}} , the imputation network produces a completed representation: X ^ = M ⊙ X + ( 1 − M ) ⊙ ( Z ref + α ⋅ Δ ⁡ ( X , M , Z ref ) ) , \hat{X}=M\odot X+(1-M)\odot\left(Z_{\text{ref}}+\alpha\cdot\Delta(X,M,Z_{\text{ref}})\right), where Δ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \Delta(\cdot) is a learned residual correction and α \alpha is a fixed scaling factor. This formulation can be interpreted as learning task-aware deviations from a strong reference imputation, rather than predicting missing values from scratch. Reference values Z ref Z_{\text{ref}} are obtained from the best-performing baseline imputation method (selected via validation), and serve as strong initial estimates that the model refines. Numerical features are used directly after standardization. Categorical variables are encoded as one-hot vectors. Missing categorical values are initialized using reference distributions with added noise and refined during training using a Gumbel-Softmax relaxation to enable differentiable sampling. Cross-entropy loss is applied to the classifier predictions. For naturally missing values, the imputed outputs are regularized toward the reference imputations: • Mean squared error for numerical features • KL divergence for categorical distributions To encourage robustness, artificial masking is applied during training by randomly hiding observed values. The model is then trained to reconstruct these values: • Smooth L1 loss for numerical features • Cross-entropy loss for categorical features The contribution of the penalty and reconstruction terms is scaled dynamically based on prediction confidence. Confidence is estimated using the entropy of the predicted class probabilities, with lower entropy indicating higher confidence. The auxiliary losses are weighted proportionally to this confidence, encouraging stronger regularization when predictions are uncertain. Training proceeds for a fixed number of iterations with mini-batch optimization. At each iteration: • A fraction of observed entries is randomly masked (data augmentation) • Missing values are imputed using either the learned imputer or the reference baseline (with probability 0.3 0.3 ) • The classifier is trained on the resulting completed data The Gumbel-Softmax temperature is annealed during training to encourage discrete categorical predictions. Early stopping is applied based on validation accuracy. At test time, missing values are imputed using the learned imputation network and predictions are produced by the classifier.

sections.heading: Number of parameters.
sections.text: Let d d denote the input dimensionality and C C the number of classes. The model consists of a classifier and a neural imputer. The total number of parameters is: # Parameters = P classifier + P imputer , \text{\# Parameters}=P_{\text{classifier}}+P_{\text{imputer}}, where both terms depend only on d d and the network architecture, and are independent of the number of training samples.

sections.heading: Implementation details.
sections.text: We use a hidden dimension of h = 256 h=256 for the imputation network. Model parameters are initialized using Kaiming uniform for linear layers. Missing numerical entries are initialized using the reference values with additive Gaussian noise 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 0.01 2 ) \mathcal{N}(0,0.01^{2}) . For categorical features, missing values are initialized by sampling from a noisy version of the reference distribution via a softmax over perturbed log-probabilities. Observed categorical values are encoded as one-hot vectors. The scaling factor for the residual correction is fixed to α = 0.1 \alpha=0.1 . We use the Adam optimizer with learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} for the classifier and 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} for the imputer. Training is performed for up to 300 iterations with mini-batches of size 64 and early stopping based on validation accuracy with a patience of 50 50 iterations. Artificial masking is applied with probability proportional to the dataset missing rate, capped at 0.2 0.2 . The Gumbel-Softmax temperature is initialized at τ = 1.0 \tau=1.0 and annealed multiplicatively with a factor of 0.995 0.995 per iteration down to a minimum of 0.3 0.3 . The penalty and reconstruction weights are set to λ pen = 0.1 \lambda_{\text{pen}}=0.1 and λ rec = 0.1 \lambda_{\text{rec}}=0.1 . Confidence-based scaling is applied using normalized prediction entropy.

sections.text: Let n n be the number of samples, d d the input dimensionality, h h the hidden dimension, b b the batch size, and T T the number of training iterations. The method jointly trains a neural imputer and a classifier, each requiring forward and backward passes with complexity 𝒪 ⁡ ( d ​ h + h 2 ) \mathcal{O}(dh+h^{2}) per sample. The overall training complexity is: 𝒪 ⁡ ( T ⋅ n b ⋅ ( d ​ h + h 2 + d ) ) , \mathcal{O}\left(T\cdot\frac{n}{b}\cdot(dh+h^{2}+d)\right), where the additional 𝒪 ⁡ ( d ) \mathcal{O}(d) term accounts for masking, reconstruction losses, and categorical sampling. The space complexity is 𝒪 ⁡ ( n ​ d + d ​ h + h 2 ) \mathcal{O}(nd+dh+h^{2}) , dominated by storing the dataset, masks, and model parameters.

An Analysis of Robustness Under Train–Test Mismatch Maria V. Salvador Affiliation: INESC TEC Affiliation: University of Porto Email: maria.v.salvador@inesctec.pt Ana F. Sequeira Affiliation: INESC TEC Affiliation: University of Porto Email: ana.f.sequeira@inesctec.pt Jaime S Cardoso Affiliation: INESC TEC Affiliation: University of Porto Email: jaime.cardoso@inesctec.pt Abstract Missing data is a pervasive challenge in machine learning, often degrading predictive performance and complicating model deployment. Most existing approaches treat imputation as a preprocessing step independent of the downstream task, a separation that becomes problematic under train–test mismatches in missingness mechanisms or rates. We introduce a unified framework that treats missing entries as variables in a task-conditioned optimization problem. We instantiate this framework in two settings: an amortized approach for scenarios with missing data at both training and test time, and a latent optimization approach for settings where only training data is incomplete. The evaluation is conducted on 98 tabular datasets and robustness under train–test mismatches is assessed on 36 datasets. Results reveal that reconstruction error constitutes a poor proxy for predictive utility (Spearman ρ ≈ \rho\approx 0.16–0.32), and that task-aware imputation becomes critical in scenarios where classical methods fail to recover complete-data performance, achieving win rates of up to 80% in challenging train–test mismatch scenarios. 1 Introduction Missing data is a pervasive problem in real-world machine learning, with significant implications for the validity, reliability, and fairness of predictive models. In practice, data may be incomplete due to collection errors, equipment failures, participant drop-out, or reluctance to disclose sensitive information. Missing values can lead to biased estimates, reduced statistical power, and degraded performance, making their handling a critical component of any data-driven pipeline. Understanding why data is missing– the missingness mechanism– is essential. There are three main missingness mechanisms: Missing Completely At Random (MCAR), where the probability of missingness is independent of the data; Missing At Random (MAR), where the probability of missingness is independent of the missing values given the observed data; and Missing Not At Random (MNAR), where the probability of missingness depends on the unobserved values themselves [ 1 , 2 ] . These mechanisms not only influence how missing data should be modeled, but also interact with when missingness occurs in the learning pipeline. In practice, an important consideration is whether missingness occurs at inference time. In some applications, missing values appear only during training, while deployment data is clean [ 2 ] . In others, missingness persists at test time, often under shifts in mechanisms or rates [ 3 , 4 ] . These scenarios pose distinct challenges: the former primarily affects representation learning, while the latter requires robustness to distribution shift. Despite these differences, most imputation methods treat missing data as a static preprocessing problem, without explicitly accounting for when or how missingness occurs. This raises a fundamental question: to what extent does improving imputation quality translate into better predictive performance, particularly in realistic settings where missingness persists at test time or differs between training and deployment? This question leads to the primary goal of this work, which is to investigate when task-aware imputation improves predictive performance in supervised learning with missing values. Our contributions are threefold. First, we show that task-aware imputation is not universally beneficial, but instead becomes critical in challenging regimes such as distribution shift and intrinsically hard missingness settings. Second, we introduce a simple and flexible formulation that treats missing values as learnable variables jointly optimized with the predictive model, providing a common perspective that encompasses both amortized and latent approaches within a single framework. Third, through a comprehensive empirical study, we demonstrate that standard reconstruction metrics are only weakly correlated with downstream performance, highlighting the limitations of conventional evaluation protocols. 2 Related Work Approaches to handling missing data include imputation, where missing entries are filled; omission, where incomplete samples are discarded; and methods that directly operate on incomplete data [ 2 , 5 , 6 ] . In this work, we focus on imputation. Classical methods such as mean, median, and K K -NN [ 7 ] are simple and efficient but fail to capture complex dependencies. Iterative approaches such as MissForest [ 8 ] , MICE [ 9 ] , and related conditional models [ 10 ] model non-linear relationships but are computationally expensive and sensitive to design choices. HyperImpute [ 11 ] extends this paradigm through automated model and hyperparameter selection, while low-rank matrix completion methods exploit global structure [ 12 , 13 ] . Learning-based approaches such as TabPFN [ 14 ] and TabImpute [ 15 ] leverage pretrained models for fast, zero-shot imputation. Deep learning methods for tabular data, including transformer-based architectures [ 16 , 17 ] , have further advanced this direction. Several approaches model the joint data distribution using deep generative models [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 ] , learning to reconstruct missing entries through reconstruction objectives, often with masking strategies during training. While expressive, these methods typically prioritize data fidelity over downstream predictive performance. Other works incorporate additional structure into the imputation process. For instance, MIRACLE [ 27 ] models the missingness mechanism under MNAR using causal assumptions, while optimal transport-based approaches align distributions between observed and missing data [ 28 , 29 ] . Handling missing data in supervised learning has traditionally relied on two-stage pipelines, where missing values are first imputed and then used for downstream prediction. This separation can lead to suboptimal performance, as imputation is not aligned with the predictive task. Benchmark studies show that the choice of imputation method significantly affects downstream performance, particularly in terms of robustness and interpretability [ 30 ] . Moreover, standard metrics such as RMSE and MAE often fail to reflect imputation quality, as they do not capture discrepancies in the underlying data distribution. Task-aware approaches aim to address this limitation. TARImpute [ 31 ] co-optimizes imputation with clustering objectives, while OptImpute [ 32 ] formulates imputation as an optimization problem independent of downstream supervision. Deep learning methods such as GRAPE [ 33 ] and GEDI [ 34 ] propose end-to-end frameworks that jointly perform imputation and prediction, often relying on specific architectural choices such as graph-based representations. Changes in missingness mechanisms can also induce distribution shift. Domain Adaptation under Missingness Shift (DAMS) [ 3 ] shows that differences in missingness alone can invalidate standard assumptions and require adaptation, particularly when missingness indicators are unavailable. Similarly, StableMiss+ [ 4 ] studies mask distribution shifts and proposes removing unstable correlations involving the missingness mask. These works highlight two key challenges: (i) robustness under shifts in missingness mechanisms or rates, and (ii) the misalignment between imputation quality and downstream predictive performance. We address these challenges by introducing a unified formulation that treats missing values as learnable variables jointly trained with the predictive model. This perspective directly aligns imputation with the task objective, and allows us to characterize when such alignment translates into improved predictive performance. Unlike prior task-aware approaches, our formulation does not depend on specific architectures or specialized designs (e.g., graph-based models), and avoids the need for bilevel optimization. Instead, it provides a simple and flexible lens to study task-aware imputation itself, encompassing both per-sample (latent) and amortized strategies within a single formulation. Furthermore, we explicitly investigate train–test mismatches in missingness mechanisms and rates, a setting that remains largely underexplored in existing work. 3 Joint-AmortizedImpute: Task-Aware Imputation via Joint Optimization Let 𝒟 = { ( 𝐱 i , y i ) } i = 1 n \mathcal{D}=\{(\mathbf{x}_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} be a dataset of n n samples, where: • 𝐱 i ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the input feature vector for the i i -th sample, • y i ∈ 𝒴 y_{i}\in\mathcal{Y} is the corresponding label or target value, • some components of 𝐱 i \mathbf{x}_{i} may be missing. Let M ∈ { 0 , 1 } n × d M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times d} be a binary mask matrix such that: m i ​ j = { 1 if ​ x i ​ j ​ is observed , 0 if ​ x i ​ j ​ is missing . m_{ij}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }x_{ij}\text{ is observed},\\ 0&\text{if }x_{ij}\text{ is missing}.\end{cases} The learning objective is to find a function f θ : ℝ d → 𝒴 f_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y} , parameterized by θ \theta , that minimizes the expected loss: min θ ⁡ 𝔼 ( 𝐱 , y ) ∼ 𝒫 ​ [ ℓ ⁡ ( f θ ​ ( 𝐱 ) , y ) ] , \min_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x},y)\sim\mathcal{P}}\left[\ell(f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}),y)\right], (1) where ℓ \ell is a loss function and 𝒫 \mathcal{P} is the underlying data distribution. However, due to missing values, we only observe 𝐱 i obs = 𝐱 i ⊙ 𝐦 i \mathbf{x}_{i}^{\text{obs}}=\mathbf{x}_{i}\odot\mathbf{m}_{i} , and do not observe 𝐱 i u = 𝐱 i ⊙ ( 𝟏 − 𝐦 i ) \mathbf{x}_{i}^{\text{u}}=\mathbf{x}_{i}\odot(\mathbf{1}-\mathbf{m}_{i}) , where ⊙ \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. We propose to jointly optimize the predictive model and the missing values in a unified objective. Let 𝐱 obs \mathbf{x}^{\text{obs}} and 𝐱 u \mathbf{x}^{\text{u}} denote the observed and unobserved components of the input, respectively. We consider the following objective: min θ , 𝐱 u ⁡ 𝔼 ( 𝐱 obs , y ) ∼ 𝒫 obs ​ [ ℓ ⁡ ( f θ ​ ( 𝐱 obs , 𝐱 u ) , y ) ] . \min_{\theta,\mathbf{x}^{\text{u}}}\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x}^{\text{obs}},y)\sim\mathcal{P}_{\text{obs}}}\left[\ell\big(f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{\text{obs}},\mathbf{x}^{\text{u}}),y\big)\right]. (3) To regularize the solution, we introduce a penalty on the unknown components: min θ , 𝐱 u ⁡ 𝔼 ( 𝐱 obs , y ) ​ [ ℓ ⁡ ( f θ ​ ( 𝐱 obs , 𝐱 u ) , y ) ] + g ⁡ ( 𝐱 u ) , \min_{\theta,\mathbf{x}^{\text{u}}}\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x}^{\text{obs}},y)}\left[\ell(f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{\text{obs}},\mathbf{x}^{\text{u}}),y)\right]+g(\mathbf{x}^{\text{u}}), (4) where g g encodes prior assumptions about plausible imputations. Reference-based parameterization. We express missing values as deviations from a reference imputation 𝐱 ^ u \hat{\mathbf{x}}^{\text{u}} : 𝐱 u = 𝐱 ^ u + 𝜹 , \mathbf{x}^{\text{u}}=\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{\text{u}}+\boldsymbol{\delta}, (5) This parameterization can be interpreted as introducing a strong prior over plausible imputations through the reference solution. It stabilizes optimization by anchoring the search in a realistic region of the input space, while allowing task-aware corrections to refine the imputation. Moreover, it reduces the effective search space, enabling the model to focus on adjustments that improve downstream performance rather than reconstructing values from scratch. This leads to the equivalent objective: min θ , 𝜹 ⁡ 𝔼 ( 𝐱 obs , y ) ​ [ ℓ ⁡ ( f θ ​ ( 𝐱 obs , 𝐱 ^ u + 𝜹 ) , y ) ] + g ⁡ ( 𝜹 ) . \min_{\theta,\boldsymbol{\delta}}\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x}^{\text{obs}},y)}\left[\ell\big(f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{\text{obs}},\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{\text{u}}+\boldsymbol{\delta}),y\big)\right]+g(\boldsymbol{\delta}). (6) A simple choice is a quadratic regularization: g ⁡ ( 𝜹 ) = λ ​ ‖ 𝜹 ‖ 2 , g(\boldsymbol{\delta})=\lambda\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|^{2}, (7) which encourages imputations to remain close to the reference. Unified imputation operator. We define a general imputation operator: 𝐱 u = ℐ ψ ​ ( 𝐱 obs , 𝐦 , 𝐱 ^ u ) , \mathbf{x}^{\text{u}}=\mathcal{I}_{\psi}(\mathbf{x}^{\text{obs}},\mathbf{m},\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{\text{u}}), (8) where ψ \psi parameterizes how imputations are computed. This formulation yields a unified objective: min θ , ψ ⁡ 𝔼 ( 𝐱 obs , y ) ​ [ ℓ ⁡ ( f θ ​ ( 𝐱 obs , ℐ ψ ​ ( ⋅ ) ) , y ) ] + g ⁡ ( ℐ ψ ​ ( ⋅ ) ) . \min_{\theta,\psi}\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x}^{\text{obs}},y)}\left[\ell\big(f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{\text{obs}},\mathcal{I}_{\psi}(\cdot)),y\big)\right]+g(\mathcal{I}_{\psi}(\cdot)). (9) Different choices of ψ \psi recover different instantiations: • Amortized imputation (Joint-AmortizedImpute): We parameterize the imputation operator as ℐ ϕ \mathcal{I}_{\phi} , with shared parameters ϕ \phi that predict imputations from inputs. This can be interpreted as learning to approximate the optimal latent corrections 𝜹 \boldsymbol{\delta} in a single forward pass, enabling generalization to unseen data and reducing computational cost. The model is trained by minimizing: ℒ = ℒ task + λ pen ​ ℒ pen + λ rec ​ ℒ rec , \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{task}}+\lambda_{\text{pen}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{pen}}+\lambda_{\text{rec}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}}, (10) where λ pen , λ rec ≥ 0 \lambda_{\text{pen}},\lambda_{\text{rec}}\geq 0 , ℒ pen \mathcal{L}_{\text{pen}} is a regularization term and ℒ rec \mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}} is a reconstruction loss. • Non-amortized imputation (Joint-LatentImpute): We directly optimize per-sample latent variables { 𝜹 i } i = 1 n \{\boldsymbol{\delta}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} . The objective reduces to Eq. 10 with λ rec = 0 \lambda_{\text{rec}}=0 . Full methodological and implementation details of Joint-AmortizedImpute and Joint-LatentImpute are provided in Appendix A.7 and Appendix A.6 , respectively. 4 Experimental Setup We evaluate the proposed framework under two complementary settings reflecting different practical scenarios regarding the availability of missing values at inference time. In our experiments, we focus on classification tasks , therefore we use the Cross-Entropy (CE) loss. For more details on the classifier, refer to Appendix A.5 . Joint-AmortizedImpute: missingness at inference time. This constitutes our main evaluation setting. We consider three scenarios to assess robustness under distribution shifts in missingness: • Robustness under train/test mismatch. – Same mechanism, different missing rates: The missingness mechanism is fixed (either MCAR, MAR or MNAR), whereas the missing rate differs between training m r train ∈ { 0.1 , 0.3 } m_{r}^{\text{train}}\in\{0.1,0.3\} and testing m r test ∈ { 0.1 , 0.3 , 0.5 , 0.7 } : m r test ≠ m r train m_{r}^{\text{test}}\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7\}:m_{r}^{\text{test}}\neq m_{r}^{\text{train}} . – Different mechanism, same missing rate: The missing rate is fixed ( m r train = m r test ∈ { 0.1 , 0.5 } m_{r}^{\text{train}}=m_{r}^{\text{test}}\in\{0.1,0.5\} ), while the missingness mechanism varies between training and testing (MCAR, MAR or MNAR). • Overall stability. Training and test data share the same missingness mechanism and rate. We evaluate six missignness mechanisms– MCAR; MAR and its sequential variant; MNAR, and its latent-factor and polarization variants– across five missing rates, m r ∈ { 0.1 , 0.3 , 0.5 , 0.7 , 0.8 } m_{r}\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.8\} . Joint-LatentImpute: no missingness at inference time. This setting isolates the effect of task-aware imputation during training while reflecting scenarios where training data is incomplete but deployment data is clean. We evaluate across the same six missingness mechanisms (MCAR; MAR and its sequential variant; and MNAR with latent-factor and polarization variants) and five missing rates m r ∈ { 0.1 , 0.3 , 0.5 , 0.7 , 0.8 } m_{r}\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.8\} . Please, refer to Appendix A.3 for more details on data splits and simulated missingness mechanisms. Baselines. We compare the proposed approach with the following imputation methods : mean/median for continuous variables, mode for categorical variables, K K -NN using the mean of the nearest neighbors for numerical variables and mode imputation for categorical ones, MissForest and TabImpute. We also consider the complete data baseline, which provides an upper bound on performance and allows us to quantify the impact of missingness and imputation. Reference imputation choice. We select the reference imputation 𝐱 ^ u \hat{\mathbf{x}}^{\text{u}} using a task-driven procedure: each candidate method is used to impute the training data, a downstream classifier is trained, and the method yielding the best validation performance is chosen. This selection is performed per dataset and missingness setting and provides a strong initialization for the proposed method, improving stability and focusing learning on task-relevant corrections. Evaluation metrics. Imputation quality is measured using Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) for numerical features and error rate for categorical features (Cat. Err.). To assess downstream utility, we train a classifier on the imputed data and report accuracy/F1-score. We report the performance gap relative to the complete-data baseline: Gap = Accuracy complete-data − Accuracy method . \mathrm{Gap}=\mathrm{Accuracy}_{\text{complete-data}}-\mathrm{Accuracy}_{\text{method}}. (11) Lower values indicate better performance, with a gap of zero corresponding to perfect recovery. We additionally measure performance recovery using the recovery ratio , defined as the ratio between the accuracy obtained under missing data and the accuracy achieved on the corresponding complete-data baseline: RR = Accuracy method Accuracy complete-data . \mathrm{RR}=\frac{\mathrm{Accuracy}_{\text{method}}}{\mathrm{Accuracy}_{\text{complete-data}}}. (12) A value of RR = 1 \mathrm{RR}=1 indicates full recovery of complete-data performance, while lower values reflect degradation due to missingness. Values greater than 1 indicate that the method outperforms the complete-data baseline. We define the hardness of a scenario based on the recovery ratio as: Hardness = 1 − RR . \mathrm{Hardness}=1-\mathrm{RR}. (13) We define four hardness levels: Easy ( Hardness < 0.02 \mathrm{Hardness}<0.02 ), Mild ( 0.02 ≤ Hardness < 0.05 0.02\leq\mathrm{Hardness}<0.05 ), Hard ( 0.05 ≤ Hardness < 0.1 0.05\leq\mathrm{Hardness}<0.1 ), and Severe ( Hardness ≥ 0.1 \mathrm{Hardness}\geq 0.1 ). Best classical method. For reporting purposes, we define the best classical method in each scenario as the imputation approach achieving the highest test accuracy. This definition is used only for post-hoc comparison and does not affect model selection, which is performed using validation performance. Datasets and data preprocessing. We evaluate our approach on classification datasets from OpenML [ 35 ] . For experiments involving distribution shifts (cross-mechanism and varying missing-rate), we use a set of 36 datasets with imbalance ratio below 10 to avoid severely skewed class distributions. In this setting, classification performance is evaluated using accuracy. To assess overall robustness and stability, including hardness analysis unrelated to distribution shifts, we extend the evaluation to a broader collection of 98 datasets. All methods are evaluated on identical data splits to ensure fair comparison. Numerical features are standardized using z-score normalization, where statistics are computed using only observed values from the training set. Further details on dataset characteristics and domains are provided in Appendix 11 . Statistical analysis. To assess statistical significance across multiple datasets, we follow standard protocols for comparing learning algorithms. Methods are ranked per dataset and compared using the Friedman test, followed by the Nemenyi post-hoc test to identify significant differences in average rank. We visualize results using critical difference (CD) diagrams, where lower ranks indicate better performance and horizontal bars connect methods that are not significantly different. Additionally, we report Spearman rank correlations to analyze the relationship between reconstruction quality and downstream performance. This work studies the role of task-aware imputation in supervised learning with missing data, with a focus on understanding when it improves predictive performance. Our results show that task-aware imputation does not uniformly improve predictive performance, but instead provides benefits primarily in challenging regimes , particularly under distribution shift and in MNAR settings, where classical methods fail to recover complete-data performance. We further find that reconstruction quality is only weakly correlated with downstream performance (Spearman ρ ≈ \rho\approx 0.16–0.32), suggesting that optimizing imputation for reconstruction alone is insufficient. These results indicate that imputation should be treated as a task-dependent problem , rather than a preprocessing step focused solely on data fidelity. Limitations and Future Work. The proposed Joint-AmortizedImpute approach uses fixed hyperparameters across all datasets. While this ensures consistent evaluation, it may limit adaptability; dataset-specific tuning or automated optimization could improve performance and robustness. The experimental comparison is also limited to a small set of baseline methods, and extending the benchmark would enable a more comprehensive evaluation. Furthermore, experiments focus exclusively on tabular classification, leaving generalization to other settings (e.g., regression or structured data such as time series) as an open question. Finally, the method does not explicitly model the missingness mechanism, which may reduce effectiveness when missingness is structured or informative. Incorporating mechanism-aware components is a promising direction for future work. Broader impacts. Improved handling of missing data can enhance the reliability of machine learning systems in real-world applications such as healthcare, finance, and scientific analysis. By aligning imputation with predictive objectives, the proposed approach may support better decision-making. However, task-aware imputation may also amplify biases in the observed data, leading to unfair or misleading outcomes, particularly in sensitive domains. Future work should explore fairness-aware imputation and develop safeguards to mitigate these risks. References [1] K. Kleinke, J. Reinecke, D. Salfrán, and M.
